extracted.intended_audience: law students, patent practitioners, and judges studying/handling patent litigation
extracted.subtask_description: Identification and analysis of the substantive and procedural defenses available to defendants in patent infringement actions (what factual and legal propositions, if proved, will bar recovery). Focused on common-law and statutory defenses as explained in a treatise on U.S. patent law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of pleadings / essential averments in declaration
rubrics_metrics.description: A general demurrer will not be sustained if the declaration substantially includes the five essential averments and does not mislead the defendant or preclude him from making under subsequent pleadings those defences which are open to him by the law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The declaration's first averment requires seven facts to concur (see separate entry). Each averment must be found true to support plaintiff's recovery; defects of form are easily remedied by amendment. Courts will not sustain a demurrer merely because of imperfection in statement or arrangement if the essential averments are substantially present.

rubrics_metrics.name: First averment (elements required for plaintiff's prima facie case)
rubrics_metrics.description: The first averment is true only when seven different facts concur: (1) the alleged invention is the result of an inventive act; (2) that inventive act was performed by the patentee or his assignor; (3) its performance by patentee/assignor preceded performance by any other person in this country; (4) the alleged invention is embraced within one of the classes of inventions made patentable by the acts of Congress; (5) it is legally new; (6) it is practically useful; (7) it has not been abandoned to the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each of the seven subordinate facts is a necessary component of the first averment — denial of any one constitutes a complete defense. These items set the substantive thresholds for entitlement to relief on a patent claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second averment (patent document / formal status of patent)
rubrics_metrics.description: The second averment is true only when nine facts exist: (1) the patent described has actually been issued by the government; (2) it was issued in the mode provided by law; (3) the invention it purports to protect is, on its face, a patentable subject-matter; (4) the specification is free from fraudulent assertion or concealment; (5) the description is without ambiguity; (6) the claims do not embrace more than the actual invention or have been or may be cured by disclaimer; (7) the claims are free from ambiguity; (8) the patent has not been surrendered; (9) the patent has not been repealed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allegations about the patent document itself must be proved; issues about patent grant and claim scope are distinct from issues about the invention's merits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third averment (ownership and right to sue)
rubrics_metrics.description: The third averment is true only when the plaintiff was the legal owner of the patent at the date of the infringement, or at the date of commencement of the suit was the legal owner and the assignee of the right of action for the infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ownership, assignment, and standing are discrete elements and if denied and proved false, defeat recovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fourth and fifth averments (infringing act and damages implied)
rubrics_metrics.description: The fourth averment is true only when four facts concur: (1) the identical invention protected by the patent has been made, used, or sold; (2) the act was performed by the defendant (alone or with others); (3) the act was performed while the patent was in force; (4) it was performed without authority from the owner. The fifth averment tenders no issue, its truth being implied by law to an extent sufficient to secure a verdict for some damages if other averments established.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof of each factual element of infringement is required; some damages may be implied by law once infringement is established.

rubrics_metrics.name: First defence: patent lacks inventive act (non-inventive / mere effect or function / not reduced to practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Defence that the alleged invention is not the result of an inventive act. An inventive act may be (1) discovery of a new force or capability and its practical application; (2) discovery of a new object or susceptibility and rendering it useful; (3) discovery and practical embodiment of a new mode of application. If the alleged invention is merely an effect or function, results from imitation rather than original discovery, or has never been made practically available, no complete inventive act exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This defence is subdivided into: (1) mere effect; (2) mere function; (3) no exercise of original discovery (imitation); (4) never practically available. Courts may take judicial notice where, from their knowledge of the art, it is apparent no inventive act was performed. Demurrer should not be sustained on patentability grounds unless matter is so evident that no question of fact exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second defence: invention not performed by the patentee (derivation/surreptitious procurement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Denial that the inventive act was performed by the patentee or his assignor — i.e., the patentee surreptitiously or unjustly appropriated another's invention and patented it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The defence does not require proof of fraud or wilful deceit — an honest but mistaken appropriator may still be not a true inventor. The statutory language 'surreptitiously' has evolved into the broader concept of 'unjustly' obtaining the patent. This defence is distinct from estoppel and from the third defence (prior invention).

rubrics_metrics.name: Third defence: patentee was not first inventor (prior invention / due diligence / interference issues)
rubrics_metrics.description: Denial that the alleged inventor performed the inventive act earlier than any other inventors in the country. This can be shown either by (1) rival inventors having conceived the idea and using due diligence in reducing it to practice at the time the patentee conceived it; or (2) the patentee having conceived first but not exercising due diligence to reduce to practice and a later conceiver perfected it sooner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This raises issues similar to Patent Office interference proceedings and equity actions; proof of prior invention or lack of diligence defeats the patentee's claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fourth defence: invention not within patentable classes / mere aggregation
rubrics_metrics.description: Denial that the invention falls within the classes protected by the acts of Congress (art, machine, manufacture, composition of matter, design, improvement) or that the claimed combination is in reality only a mere aggregation of independent elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the nature of the invention is apparent from the description and claims, the court may take judicial notice and refuse to entertain the action if the result, though new and useful, is not legally patentable under statutory classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fifth defence: lack of legal novelty (prior use, prior patent, prior publication)
rubrics_metrics.description: Denial that the invention is new within the meaning of the law. Novelty is lacking (the invention is legally old) if before the date of conception or application there was: (a) practical employment of the identical invention in the United States in a manner accessible to the public (prior use); (b) a prior patent issued to the public containing a full enabling disclosure of the identical invention (prior patent); (c) a prior printed publication that disclosed essential characteristics enabling skilled persons to construct and apply the invention (prior publication).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are three distinct complete defenses; when any is established by sufficient proof the invention is legally old and the patent invalid. The existence of these conditions is a conclusion of law once proven. Prior use, patent, and publication each have specific evidentiary and temporal requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sixth defence: lack of utility
rubrics_metrics.description: Denial that the invention is useful. An invention is useful if available for any use which overall benefits the public. Utterly frivolous or worthless inventions have no utility. An invention whose practice is inevitably more injurious than beneficial, or prejudicial to the public, lacks utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Want of utility is a per se defence; evidence must show the invention is utterly worthless. Defendants who have actually practiced the invention (or induced public purchase) are estopped from asserting lack of utility against the patentee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seventh defence: abandonment / dedication to the public
rubrics_metrics.description: Averment that the invention was abandoned to the public before the acts constituting infringement. Abandonment assumes the invention was complete and practically operative and intentionally and unreservedly surrendered to the public by its owner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public use or sale by the inventor (or with his consent) for more than two years before the patent application is conclusive evidence of abandonment. Other conduct may permit an inference of intent to abandon but is rebuttable. Experimental uses or sales restricted by conditions enforceable by the inventor do not constitute abandonment. Distinguish abandonment by public use/sale (conclusive) from abandonment by other conduct (inferential).

rubrics_metrics.name: Eighth defence: patent never granted / patent incorrectly pleaded
rubrics_metrics.description: Denial that the letters-patent described in the declaration were ever granted by the government or that the patent described is not correctly set forth in the declaration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This defence challenges the existence or correct recital of the patent instrument (equivalent to nul del record). Any material variance between the actual patent and the declaration can defeat the action unless cured by amendment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ninth defence: patent issued not in conformity with law (procedural/formal defects in issuance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Denial that the patent, though issued, was issued in accordance with the formal requirements of the law — e.g., issued upon a false oath or suggestion, lacking required signatures or seal, departing from the application, or purporting to secure rights to someone other than the applicant or lawful assignee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many informalities (omission of oath or fee, minor attestations) are cured by allowance of the patent and cannot be collaterally attacked; courts generally will not review Patent Office action on certain prerequisites. However, serious faults (false oath, lack of signatures/seal, patent claiming different invention/owner than application) may be raised in defense to infringement. The unintentional issue of a patent is not a defense; only certain substantial irregularities are actionable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defenses beyond statutory enumeration (violations in granting patent / questions of law)
rubrics_metrics.description: Defences are not limited to those named in statute but embrace all violations of law in granting the patent — such violations raise questions of law on which the decision of the Commissioner is not necessarily final.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts may consider legal defects in the grant process that go beyond mere formalities; some such issues may be reviewable despite the general finality of Patent Office actions on certain matters.
